employee-vs-consultant.core: Employees trade time for salary, benefits and stability; consultants sell outcomes or expertise to many clients, earning higher rates but carrying sales, admin, gaps between contracts, self-funded benefits and business risk. Consulting rewards deep, in-demand expertise and a network that sends referrals.

first_principles.problem: An engineer quits to consult at 2× their hourly salary equivalent and is surprised to earn less overall.
truths: Consultants aren't billable 100% of the time.
Benefits, taxes and tools are self-funded.
Sales and admin take real hours.
derivation: Compute **effective rate** = revenue ÷ total hours (incl. sales/admin).

analogy.title: A salaried chef versus a caterer
analogy.story: The caterer charges more per event but finds clients, buys equipment and has quiet weeks.
analogy.breaks: Caterers have physical limits; expertise consultants can scale with productised offers.

check.q: Why must consultants charge much more than their salary's hourly equivalent?
check.a: They're not fully utilised and must cover benefits, taxes, sales time and gaps between contracts.

pricing-models-hourly-vs-retainer-vs-pro.core: Hourly billing is simple but caps income and punishes efficiency. Retainers buy guaranteed access monthly and give predictable revenue. Fixed project fees price the outcome, rewarding expertise and speed but carrying scope risk. Value-based pricing ties fees to the client's gain.

first_principles.problem: An expert who fixes a $1M/year problem in two days earns only 16 hours' pay.

analogy.title: A plumber's call-out rate versus an annual service plan versus a fixed bathroom install
analogy.story: Each pays differently for different kinds of work.
analogy.breaks: Plumbing scope is visible; software scope creeps invisibly.

check.q: What's the main risk of a fixed project fee?
check.a: Scope creep: extra work without extra pay unless a change process is defined.

the-statement-of-work-sow.core: A Statement of Work defines the engagement: objectives, scope (and explicit out-of-scope items), deliverables, timeline, acceptance criteria, assumptions, client responsibilities, fees, payment terms and change-request process. It prevents misaligned expectations and disputes.

first_principles.problem: A 'quick CI setup' grows into rewriting the client's test suite, unpaid.

analogy.title: Architect's drawings for a house extension
analogy.story: Everyone agrees exactly what will be built before work starts.
analogy.breaks: Drawings are precise; software requirements always have some uncertainty, so include assumptions.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Test-suite work becomes a separate paid change.

code.text:
## Objective: CI pipeline for 3 services
## Deliverables: GitHub Actions workflows, docs, handover session
## Out of scope: fixing existing failing tests
## Acceptance: green build < 10 min on main
## Fee: $18k, 50% upfront, 50% on acceptance
## Changes: written request, quoted separately

check.a: It prevents assumptions that adjacent work is included, reducing scope creep and disputes.

advisory-board-roles.core: Startup advisors offer periodic expertise, introductions and credibility, usually for small equity (≈0.1–1%) vesting over 1–2 years, sometimes with cash. Good advisory relationships have clear expectations (hours/month, areas), a written agreement and genuine alignment with the founders' needs.

first_principles.problem: An engineer becomes an 'advisor' with no defined role and is never consulted again.
truths: Advisors trade time and network for equity.
derivation: Watch **conflicts of interest** with your employer.

analogy.title: A trusted family doctor on call
analogy.story: Not daily care, but available for key decisions and referrals.
analogy.breaks: Doctors are paid per visit; advisors are often paid in uncertain equity.

check.q: What should you check with your employer before advising a startup?
check.a: Conflict-of-interest and outside-activity policies, especially for competitors or IP overlap.

finding-and-closing-consulting-clients.core: Most consulting work comes from referrals and visible expertise, not cold outreach: former colleagues, content that demonstrates skill, and a narrow positioning ('I fix Kubernetes cost overruns for Series B startups'). Close with discovery calls focused on the client's problem, a clear proposal with options, and fast follow-up.

first_principles.problem: A new consultant sends hundreds of cold emails and lands nothing.
truths: Clients buy solutions to painful problems.

analogy.title: A specialist surgeon's referral network
analogy.story: GPs send patients to the specialist they trust for that specific problem.
analogy.breaks: Patients must see a specialist; clients can always choose to do nothing.

example.title: First three clients
flow: Post: 'Now helping startups cut cloud costs'
Two inbound leads from the post

check.q: Why does a narrow niche help consultants?
check.a: It makes you easy to remember and refer, and clients trust specialists with their specific problem.
